prompt: I'm a solo SaaS founder with no GEO budget. How can I tell whether an AI visibility score for ChatGPT and Grok is trustworthy?
submitted_time_reported: User confirmed manually sent before first observation; exact click time unavailable.
answer_text:
How to tell whether an AI visibility score is trustworthy (without a GEO budget)

My short answer: Don't trust the score. Trust the measurement process behind the score.

As a solo SaaS founder, you don't need an expensive GEO platform to evaluate whether ChatGPT or Grok recommends your product. You need to know:

What questions were asked?

How many times were they asked?

What exactly counts as visibility?

Can you reproduce the results yourself?

AI visibility is not like traditional Google rankings. The same AI assistant can give different answers to the same question depending on the session, search behavior, location, and time. Research published in 2026 also highlights how single-run visibility measurements can produce misleading rankings. 
arXiv
+1

Here's the practical framework I'd use.

1. The six tests of a trustworthy AI visibility score

Test

	

Trustworthy measurement

	

Red flag




Prompt transparency

	

Shows the exact questions

	

Says it uses proprietary prompts




Repeatability

	

Runs each prompt multiple times

	

One answer per prompt




Engine separation

	

Separate ChatGPT and Grok scores

	

One blended AI score




Evidence

	

Stores actual answers and URLs

	

Only displays a number




Scoring clarity

	

Explains its formula and denominator

	

Proprietary score from 0–100




Uncertainty

	

Shows variability over time

	

Claims a 3-point increase is significant

A particularly important distinction: a tool that reports a score of 72/100 hasn't necessarily measured 72% visibility.

It might have assigned arbitrary weights to:

Brand mentions

Citation frequency

Position in the answer

Sentiment

Competitor comparisons

Unless you can see the formula, you cannot interpret the score.

2. Check whether the score measures the right thing

There are three different outcomes that GEO tools often combine.

Metric 1

Brand mention rate

Does ChatGPT or Grok mention your SaaS at all?

Example: 8 out of 30 answers mention your product = 26.7%.

Metric 2

Recommendation rate

Does the AI actually recommend your product as a solution?

Being mentioned in a list of ten tools is not the same as being recommended as the best fit.

Metric 3

Citation rate

Does the AI cite your website or another source that identifies your product?

This helps you understand whether your content is being surfaced as a source, rather than merely whether your brand name appears.

My recommendation: Track all three separately.

For a small SaaS, recommendation rate may be more commercially useful than a generic visibility score.

For example:

70% mention rate, but only 5% recommendation rate: you're known, but not necessarily competitive.

20% mention rate, but 15% recommendation rate: you're less frequently mentioned, but often a strong fit when you appear.

0% official-site citation rate: investigate whether your content is being discovered and cited, even if the brand is mentioned elsewhere.

Also record your position in the answer (first recommendation, top three, or mentioned later).

3. Make sure ChatGPT and Grok are actually being tested correctly

This is an important technical detail that many founders overlook.

ChatGPT

ChatGPT can automatically search the web when a question benefits from current information. Its search behavior can also involve location information and external search providers. 
OpenAI Help Center
+1

A trustworthy report should disclose whether it tests:

ChatGPT's consumer-facing interface.

ChatGPT with web search enabled.

An OpenAI API model without web search.

An API model with web search.

These are different measurement environments.

Grok

The same distinction applies to Grok.

xAI documents a web-search tool for its API, including the ability to retrieve citations from sources encountered during searches. 
SpaceXSI Docs
+1

Ask whether the vendor tests:

The actual Grok user experience at grok.com.

An xAI API model.

An API model with web search enabled.

An API model without web search.

An API-based Grok result should not automatically be presented as proof of visibility in the consumer-facing Grok experience.

A useful vendor question:

"Are you testing the actual ChatGPT and Grok interfaces, or querying their APIs? What model versions, search settings, and account conditions do you use?"

If they can't answer, downgrade your confidence in the score.

4. Test the score yourself for free

You can do a surprisingly useful audit without purchasing any GEO software.

I'd start with 10 real buyer questions, three independent runs per question, on each platform.

That's 60 responses in total.

Build your prompt list

Don't just ask whether AI knows your brand. Test whether it recommends you when a potential customer needs your solution.

Here are example prompt patterns for a SaaS business:

Category

	

Example prompt




Category discovery

	

Best [category] software for small businesses




Problem solving

	

How can I solve [customer problem] without hiring a developer?




Use case

	

What tools help automate [specific workflow]?




Alternatives

	

What are good alternatives to [competitor]?




Comparison

	

Compare [your product] with [competitor]




Budget

	

Best affordable [category] tools for startups




Integration

	

Which [category] tools integrate with [popular platform]?

Use actual buyer language wherever possible.

I'd allocate your initial ten prompts roughly as follows:

6 non-branded discovery questions.

2 competitor/alternative questions.

2 questions explicitly mentioning your brand.

Keep branded questions separate when calculating discovery visibility. Otherwise, you're rewarding the system for already being told your name.

Run the experiment

Open ChatGPT and Grok separately.

Start a fresh conversation for every run.

Use the exact same prompt each time.

Record the answer, date, model/interface, and citations.

Repeat each prompt three times, ideally across different days.

Don't change the prompt list halfway through the experiment.

Keep the region, language, and search settings consistent. If you sell internationally, run separate tests for important markets rather than mixing them.

Interpretation: ChatGPT currently produces more visibility in this sample. This is a directional observation, not proof that ChatGPT is inherently a better acquisition channel.

One statistical warning: 30 responses per platform is a useful starting experiment, not a robust market-wide estimate. A 2026 research paper found substantial citation variability, with apparently different visibility figures sometimes falling within the statistical noise. 
arXiv
+1

Repeat the experiment weekly before interpreting small changes as improvements.

6. Five questions to ask any GEO vendor before paying

Copy these questions and send them to a vendor offering an AI visibility score.

Questions about your AI visibility measurement methodology
\u53d1\u9001
\u6536\u4ef6\u4eba

Hi,

I'm evaluating AI visibility tracking for my SaaS product, particularly across ChatGPT and Grok.

Before considering a subscription, I'd like to understand your measurement methodology.

Could you clarify:

What exact prompts do you use to calculate my visibility score?

How many times is each prompt tested per platform?

Do you test the actual consumer-facing ChatGPT and Grok interfaces, or their APIs?

Can I access the raw AI responses, timestamps, and citation URLs?

How do you calculate the score, and do you provide separate mention, recommendation, and citation rates?

How do you account for response variability, model updates, and geographic differences?

Can you demonstrate that a change in my score is statistically meaningful rather than normal output variation?

I'm particularly interested in reproducibility and the ability to independently verify the reported numbers.

Thanks!

If the vendor answers these questions transparently, that's a positive sign. If it only shows an attractive dashboard with a proprietary score, be cautious.

7. What I'd prioritize as a zero-budget SaaS founder

Don't spend your limited time chasing a score from 35 to 65.

I'd prioritize these activities:

Priority

	

Activity

	

Why




1

	

Test 10–20 buyer-intent prompts

	

Establish your baseline




2

	

Identify which competitors get recommended

	

Find your competitive gaps




3

	

Inspect cited sources

	

Discover where AI gets its information




4

	

Improve your comparison and use-case pages

	

Make your positioning easier to understand




5

	

Repeat the same tests weekly

	

Check whether changes persist

One additional technical check: make sure your website isn't accidentally blocking OpenAI's OAI-SearchBot. OpenAI documents that this crawler is used to surface websites in ChatGPT search results. Allowing it doesn't guarantee a recommendation, but blocking it can prevent your pages from appearing in those search results. 
OpenAI Developers
+1

My final verdict: a simple trust scale

Level 1 — Marketing metric

Low trust

Score from 0–100, no disclosed prompts, no raw answers.

Level 2 — Directional metric

Moderate trust

Disclosed prompts, platform breakdown, actual responses, but limited repeat sampling.

Level 3 — Reproducible metric

Higher trust

Exact prompts, multiple runs, raw outputs, citations, scoring formula, model/interface details, and uncertainty reporting.

The most important principle:

AI visibility is an observation, not a business outcome.

A high score doesn't prove that customers are discovering you, clicking through, or buying. Eventually, connect your observations to referral traffic, signups, and conversions. Don't confuse visibility with revenue.

One thing I'd like to help you with next
